newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya state radio warns public against rallies.
newsitem.headline: Kenya state radio warns public against rallies.

text.p: State radio warned Kenyans on Saturday against attending outlawed rallies called across the country for Monday by groups demanding constitutional reforms.
The radio repeatedly broadcast a police statement saying the rallies were illegal and asking peace-loving citizens to keep away from some 50 venues named by organisers.
The radio also quoted President Daniel arap Moi as saying on Saturday that law enforcement agencies would be out in full force in Kenya on Monday to prevent the rallies going ahead.
Kenya's National Council of NGOs meanwhile said on Saturday it was being intimidated because its staff had been put under surveillance in recent weeks and its telephones were tapped.
But executive committee members of the National Council of NGOs (Non-Governmental Organisations) said its registration could not be withdrawn, as threatened by Moi, as it was never registered.
Opposition groups and other bodies, including the National Council of NGOs, demanding constitutional reforms before this year's general election have called the rallies for Monday.

The pro-reform groups reiterated on Saturday that Monday's rallies would be "educational meetings" and argued they therefore do not need police permission. They said they had even formally requested police protection for the meetings.

The executive committee members said the National Council of NGOs was a statutory body set up by parliament in 1993 as a forum for all registered NGOs in Kenya and was not required to be registered itself.
On Friday, Moi warned Kenyans to avoid what he said was a new culture of violence in Kenya and singled out the National Council of NGOs for meddling in politics and formenting trouble.
He said the government would not hesitate to deregister the council if it continued with its interference. Parties and other bodies which are denied official registration cannot operate.
Moi says there is no time for constitutional reforms before the presidential and parliamentary elections this year. The date for the general election has not yet been set.
The secretary-general of the opposition FORD-Kenya party said on Saturday homes of leading opposition figures were under surveillance from the paramilitary General Service Unit (GSU).

"All indications are that the Kenya police are determined to disrupt the orderly conduct of the major political event (on Monday) under the guise of maintaining law and order," FORD -Kenya Secretary-General Gitobu Imanyara said in a statement.
He said the GSU surveillance indicated that the police planned to imprison opposition leaders in their homes on Monday to stop them reaching the rallies -- as happened on May 31.
In Kenya's port city of Mombasa on Saturday, a lawyer said police on Friday arrested three activists who had allegedly distributed leaflets calling for a general strike on Monday.
Lawyer Lumatete Muchai said he was still trying to locate one of the three men, who was his client, but he doubted that he would be released until Tuesday. Police refused to comment.
Despite the opposition campaign, Moi, 73, looks certain to extend his 19-year rule for five more years because of electoral rules and deep personal and ethnic splits within the opposition.
